new.name: category_attention_vs_bounce
new.mechanism: View counts treat a 2-second bounce and a 4-minute read the same way. Page dwell is the time to the next event in the session, capped at 300s, on a log scale. Two baselines are subtracted from each of the user's views in the last 48h: the category's mean log dwell over all users in the same 48h, which removes page-type effects (spec-heavy electronics versus accessories), and the user's own mean residual, which removes reading speed. The family is the shrunk mean of what remains, per user and each of the latest 3 categories. A positive value marks the category where this user reads longer than the user and the category normally do: evaluation in earnest, the comparison phase ripe to convert. Three changes answer the critiques. Session-final views, which have no measurable dwell, are now excluded from both numerator and denominator, which removes the recency artifact. new.mechanism: Session-kNN, the classic session-based recommender. The user's latest session (all its distinct items) is matched against other users' 7d sessions of 2-20 items by set-overlap cosine, indexing up to 200 most recent sessions per item. The 15 most similar sessions vote for their items with similarity weight. Existing cf_ columns aggregate pairwise item-item links, so a candidate weakly linked to each of several current items cannot beat one strongly linked to a single item. Session-kNN rewards items that co-occur with the user's whole intent bundle, which the next-day first cart tends to complete. Revision: the family is now restricted to users whose current session holds at least 2 items, where the set match differs from pairwise co-view. The per-item index is computed only for the items of current sessions. Values are unchanged, because the window partitions by product, and cost falls. The acquisition column is now the candidate's share of the neighbours' acquisition mass (sum sim*acq over the user's total sim*acq), so a uniform change in the day's cart level cancels out. The view column is the similarity-weighted vote share.

new.name: coview_pure_two_hop_diffusion
new.mechanism: Two-step diffusion over the 7d session co-view graph, now restricted to items the user's seeds reach ONLY through a second hop. The first hop from each of the user's 5 latest 48h views (weighted 1/rank) takes the seed's top 10 neighbours by cosine, with no minimum count, so thin-edge niche seeds still reach intermediates. The second hop takes each intermediate's top 10 neighbours by cosine among edges with at least 2 co-sessions. Every candidate that was ever co-viewed in a 7d session with any of the user's seeds is removed. That drops the one-hop items that existing co-view columns already score, which was the cause of R2 0.6 to the co-view source rank. What remains are items in the user's comparison cluster that were never compared directly with what the user looked at. Two columns are emitted: the log diffused probability and the log number of distinct paths, which marks cluster centrality. The top-60 cut per user is ordered by the probability rounded to 6 decimals, then hash, so float summation order cannot flip keys.

new.name: session_forward_flow_direction
new.mechanism: Direction of browsing flow. In 7d view sessions of 2-30 items, for each co-viewed pair (a, b) the family counts sessions where b was first viewed after a (forward) versus before a (backward), over the whole session rather than only the next click. It is applied from the user's 5 latest 48h views. Critics showed the raw forward share mostly encoded item-level downstreamness: bestsellers are entry points, so it tracked inverse popularity (R2 0.45 to s_pop_rank). Revision: the forward column is now an excess. It is the smoothed pooled pair forward share minus the candidate's own baseline share of co-session items viewed before it, over all its 7d sessions. Item-level position and popularity cancel out. What remains is whether people go from THIS user's current items to the candidate more often than they reach it from anything else, which is pair-specific downstream intent. The signed log net flow is kept. It is view-only, so the cart level cannot move it.

new.name: uc_category_reacquisition_hazard
new.mechanism: Some targets lie far from the latest views. A user who acquired in category c some days ago comes back to acquire another new item of c (consumables, accessories in series, gifts), often without fresh browsing of c, so the recency-decayed uc_ and cf_ signals are weak. This family learns from 14 days the category-specific daily hazard of a new-item acquisition in c at lag L days after the previous acquisition day in c. L is bucketed as 1, 2, 3-4 and 5-13; the former 8-13 bucket was merged because it was thin and holiday-dominated at early anchors. The hazard is evaluated at the user's own current lag in each category they acquired in and attached to the top 30 acquired products of that category. Column 1 is the hazard against the overall at-risk rate. Column 2 is the category excess over the global hazard at the same lag; both are ratios, so the daily cart level largely cancels. cards.name: consideration_set_price_drift
cards.mechanism: During the comparison phase, the user's own set of items considered in a category in the last 48h defines a live price frame, and users who trade up or down usually finish past their latest views. The percentile column, a 48h copy of up_cat_logratio_med (R2 0.735), is dropped. Only the drift alignment is kept: the mean log price of the more recent half of the considered items minus that of the earlier half, multiplied by the candidate's offset from the set mean and scaled by the set's spread. It is positive when the candidate lies in the direction the user is moving. A static distance to the median cannot express this. Two changes answer the critiques. The candidate price is now the mean log price over 7 days rather than the tie-dependent last price, so it is less sensitive to promos. Pairs now cover each of the user's latest 3 categories crossed with the union of the top 30 acquired and top 30 most-viewed-in-48h items, which reaches more of the items the user is actually comparing.

The re-views-per-item column, which overlapped uc_share_hl1d and r2p4, is dropped. cards.name: category_attention_vs_bounce
cards.mechanism: View counts treat a 2-second bounce and a 4-minute read the same way. Page dwell is the time to the next event in the session, capped at 300s, on a log scale. Two baselines are subtracted from each of the user's views in the last 48h: the category's mean log dwell over all users in the same 48h, which removes page-type effects (spec-heavy electronics versus accessories), and the user's own mean residual, which removes reading speed. The family is the shrunk mean of what remains, per user and each of the latest 3 categories. A positive value marks the category where this user reads longer than the user and the category normally do: evaluation in earnest, the comparison phase ripe to convert. Three changes answer the critiques. Session-final views, which have no measurable dwell, are now excluded from both numerator and denominator, which removes the recency artifact. The bounce column, ambiguous in sign and mostly not about timing, is dropped. The category baseline addresses the page-type rival directly. The family uses views only, so it is robust to the cart level.

cards.name: lifecycle_phase
cards.mechanism: Products move through a life cycle: launch, ramp-up, peak, then decline. The existing trend columns compare the last day with a 7-day average, and i_is_fresh_item_7d is only a binary flag. This family places each item on its own 14-day curve with two columns. The first is how many days ago the item's traffic-normalised daily viewer share peaked. The second is how far yesterday's share sits below that peak, as a log gap. Shares are distinct viewers over global distinct users per day, so shifts in traffic and cart logging cancel. Items at or near their peak should become next-day first acquisitions more often than items of the same current popularity that peaked a week ago and are fading. Revision: the CTE alias fs is renamed. The age column is dropped because it is censored at the window start and duplicates i_is_fresh_item_7d and other first-seen columns.

cards.mechanism: One-day-versus-seven-day ratios cannot tell sustained growth from a single spike, such as a logging glitch or a one-off push. The view column is the similarity-weighted vote share.

cards.mechanism: Two-step diffusion over the 7d session co-view graph, now restricted to items the user's seeds reach ONLY through a second hop. The first hop from each of the user's 5 latest 48h views (weighted 1/rank) takes the seed's top 10 neighbours by cosine, with no minimum count, so thin-edge niche seeds still reach intermediates. The second hop takes each intermediate's top 10 neighbours by cosine among edges with at least 2 co-sessions. That drops the one-hop items that existing co-view columns already score, which was the cause of R2 0.6 to the co-view source rank. What remains are items in the user's comparison cluster that were never compared directly with what the user looked at. Two columns are emitted: the log diffused probability and the log number of distinct paths, which marks cluster centrality. The top-60 cut per user is ordered by the probability rounded to 6 decimals, then hash, so float summation order cannot flip keys.

cards.name: session_forward_flow_direction
cards.mechanism: Direction of browsing flow. In 7d view sessions of 2-30 items, for each co-viewed pair (a, b) the family counts sessions where b was first viewed after a (forward) versus before a (backward), over the whole session rather than only the next click. It is applied from the user's 5 latest 48h views. Critics showed the raw forward share mostly encoded item-level downstreamness: bestsellers are entry points, so it tracked inverse popularity (R2 0.45 to s_pop_rank). Revision: the forward column is now an excess. It is the smoothed pooled pair forward share minus the candidate's own baseline share of co-session items viewed before it, over all its 7d sessions. Item-level position and popularity cancel out. What remains is whether people go from THIS user's current items to the candidate more often than they reach it from anything else, which is pair-specific downstream intent. The signed log net flow is kept. It is view-only, so the cart level cannot move it.

cards.name: reverse_neighbour_recall
cards.mechanism: This reverses the direction of the item-item lookup. For each candidate, its own top 8 co-view neighbours by cosine (7d graph) are taken, and the family gives the share of that cosine mass the user touched among their 30 latest items of the last 14 days. Existing cf_ columns ask whether the candidate is in a seed's top list. That favours popular candidates, which appear in many lists. This family asks whether the user has covered the candidate's own neighbourhood, so a niche item whose few close alternatives the user already inspected scores high even when it ranks low in the seeds' lists. Revisions: the hours column was dropped, since it duplicated uc_last_h (R2 0.66). The reverse cap per touched item was raised from 40 to 100, so hub neighbours no longer silently truncate recall. The twin now keeps the exact key set and replaces the candidate's neighbourhood with that of a same-category, same-popularity-decile product. This addresses the coverage mismatch.

cards.mechanism: This is a timed transition graph. For pairs (a, b) where a user viewed a within the 72h before their first cart/purchase of b (14d), the family stores the mean log lag from the FIRST view of a in that window, which marks the start of deliberation, to the acquisition. Fast transitions (add-ons) and slow ones (big-ticket deliberation) resolve on different schedules, which untimed or fixed-decay transition columns cannot express. The category-cold column was dropped because it duplicated i_cat_multi_buy_14d (R2 0.76) and C05. The first acquisition event is chosen with a deterministic tiebreak.

cards.null_stratum: Users still browsing at the anchor, whose targets mostly fall in a continuing session: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM hist h WHERE h.user_id = u.user_id AND h.event_time >= TIMESTAMP '{t}' - INTERVAL 2 HOUR)
cards.sql: WITH h AS (SELECT user_id, user_session, product_id, event_time, event_type FROM hist WHERE event_time >= TIMESTAMP '{t}' - INTERVAL 14 DAY AND user_session IS NOT NULL AND product_id IS NOT NULL), us AS (SELECT user_id, user_session, min(event_time) AS s0, max(event_time) AS s1 FROM h GROUP BY user_id, user_session), usg AS (SELECT user_id, user_session, date_diff('minute', lag(s1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY s0, user_session), s0) AS gapm FROM us), acq AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, user_session AS sess, event_time AS acq_ts FROM h WHERE event_type IN ('cart','purchase') QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY event_time, user_session) = 1), a AS (SELECT q.product_id, CAST(g.gapm IS NULL OR g.gapm >= 1440 AS DOUBLE) AS ret, CAST(g.gapm IS NULL OR g.gapm >= 7200 AS DOUBLE) AS rlong FROM acq q JOIN usg g ON g.user_id = q.user_id AND g.user_session = q.sess WHERE q.acq_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{t}' - INTERVAL 7 DAY), gl AS (SELECT avg(ret) AS pr, avg(rlong) AS pl FROM a), p AS (SELECT product_id, count(*) AS n, sum(ret) AS sr, sum(rlong) AS sl FROM a GROUP BY product_id) SELECT p.product_id, ln((p.sr + 10 * gl.pr) / (p.n + 10) / gl.pr) AS f_x_c4_i_return_visit_acq_lift_7d, ln((p.sl + 10 * gl.pl) / (p.n + 10) / gl.pl) AS f_x_c4_i_long_gap_acq_lift_7d FROM p CROSS JOIN gl

twin.sql: WITH h AS (SELECT user_id, user_session, product_id, event_time, event_type FROM hist WHERE event_time >= TIMESTAMP '{t}' - INTERVAL 14 DAY AND user_session IS NOT NULL AND product_id IS NOT NULL), us AS (SELECT user_id, user_session, min(event_time) AS s0, max(event_time) AS s1 FROM h GROUP BY user_id, user_session), usg AS (SELECT user_id, user_session, date_diff('minute', lag(s1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY s0, user_session), s0) AS gapm FROM us), acq AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, user_session AS sess, event_time AS acq_ts FROM h WHERE event_type IN ('cart','purchase') QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY event_time, user_session) = 1), a0 AS (SELECT q.user_id, q.product_id, CAST(date_trunc('day', q.acq_ts) AS DATE) AS d, CAST(g.gapm IS NULL OR g.gapm >= 1440 AS DOUBLE) AS ret, CAST(g.gapm IS NULL OR g.gapm >= 7200 AS DOUBLE) AS rlong FROM acq q JOIN usg g ON g.user_id = q.user_id AND g.user_session = q.sess WHERE q.acq_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{t}' - INTERVAL 7 DAY), a1 AS (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY user_id, product_id) AS r1, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY d ORDER BY hash(user_id, product_id), user_id, product_id) AS r2 FROM a0), a AS (SELECT x.product_id, y.ret, y.rlong FROM a1 x JOIN a1 y ON x.d = y.d AND x.r2 = y.r1), gl AS (SELECT avg(ret) AS pr, avg(rlong) AS pl FROM a), p AS (SELECT product_id, count(*) AS n, sum(ret) AS sr, sum(rlong) AS sl FROM a GROUP BY product_id) SELECT p.product_id, ln((p.sr + 10 * gl.pr) / (p.n + 10) / gl.pr) AS f_x_c4_i_return_visit_acq_lift_7d_tw, ln((p.sl + 10 * gl.pl) / (p.n + 10) / gl.pl) AS f_x_c4_i_long_gap_acq_lift_7d_tw FROM p CROSS JOIN gl

rival.explanation: Return-session acquisitions may just mark promoted or ad-landing items, which f_x_i_new_reach_*, f_x_i_quick_acq_share_7d and i_trend_actor_1v7 already describe. The gain would then appear for all users as an item promo score, not specifically for users returning after a pause.
rival.stratum: Users still browsing at the anchor (event in the last 2h), equally with paused users

withdrawn.reason: TWIN-BROKEN with rho 0.90/0.95 to the twin. Most sessions hold a single item, so 'landing' equals presence, and the conversion column is i_cart_lift_7d (R2 0.847). Restricting to multi-item sessions would make the landing share a copy of f_x_i_last_vs_first_7d (R2 0.706). No distinct, testable signal remains.

f_x_c1_opencart_hours_log is an exact copy of uc_last_cp_h (R2 1.0), and the item count is R2 0.916 to uc_distinct_viewed_7d. The 'unresolved' flag rests on the cart-vs-purchase split, which the brief warns is unstable across days. The co-view route for abandoned carts is already covered by r6p3.

f_x_c1_cat_return_episodes_log duplicates uc_active_days_14d (R2 0.972), and the gap column is R2 0.788 to the same column. Gaps of at least 12h mostly encode the overnight and weekend rhythm. What remains is a user x category constant that does not reorder items within a category.

Both category shares are category identity: R2 0.69 and 0.65 to category cart_per_view, and the day-shuffled twin keeps R2 0.61 and 0.59. f_x_c2_wave_dlogp_vs_cat duplicates i_price_change_7d (R2 0.744). The twin is broken on coverage. A scalar that is uniform within a category also cannot rank items inside the user's main category. A wave effect that spreads along co-view edges would need a different family.

At hourly resolution the longest gap is set by traffic sparsity, not by stock-outs. f_x_c2_rs_max_gap_rel has R2 0.728 to f_x_dfs_p_purchase_u_1d, and after_vs_before reads as a short trend. The New-Year trough also adds calendar holes for the earliest anchors. A restock signal that survives these objections needs established items, a gap of at least 48h and returning viewers from before the gap. That would cover too few items to justify three columns.

The neighbour_shuffle twin uses random pseudo-groups and fits as closely as the card: R2 0.623 and 0.707 against 0.634 and 0.698 to i_trend_view_1v7 and i_trend_actor_1v7. The share columns are therefore the item's own 3v14 momentum, and the (category, brand) structure adds nothing measurable. The age percentile is censored at the window start and ties for old items. Testing succession properly would need a directional sibling-to-sibling transition, which is a different family.

The stalled shares are constant within a category and act as category conversion identity: R2 0.53 and 0.62 to category and brand buy_per_view. The time-shuffled twin keeps the same R2 (0.54 and 0.56), so the last-24h timing adds nothing measurable. For an item averaging 3 viewers a day, a silent day happens by Poisson chance alone. Substitute spillover would have to flow along co-view edges from the stalled item, which a category scalar cannot express.

Three problems, none of which a revision fixes. (1) The family is a co-view expansion of long-memory seeds, close to r5p5 and r6p1 (R2 0.31-0.33 to f_x_cf_consid_cv_wsum). (2) The persistence count is confounded with the user's number of sessions, which is the heavy-user rival. The session-reassigning twin even raised coverage, showing that spreading items over sessions alone creates the signal. (3) I see no twin that holds the support fixed while destroying cross-visit recurrence. Coverage is 3.6% and limited to heavy users, so the column is more likely to add noise than a distinct signal.

The time_shuffle twin moves each acquisition to a random event of the same user, yet it keeps rho_wq 0.88 and 0.87 with the card and nearly the same R2 (0.59 vs 0.61) to cf_tr_lift_max. The claimed post-acquisition anchoring therefore carries almost nothing. What remains is co-touch by the same acquirers within 14d, which duplicates cf_tr_lift_max and the co-acquisition families r1p2 and r2p3.

Four problems. (1) The family correlates at rho 0.969 with uc_rank_in_user and at R2 0.74 with uc_last_h, so on the ranked rows it does not isolate untouched categories as claimed; it mostly re-encodes the user-category columns. (2) Coverage is only 1.4% and falls 40% over three probe days, because the entry definition rests on a cart within 24h of the first touch, which follows the shifting cart level. (3) The category-substitution twin collapses coverage tenfold, and I see no shape-preserving control. (4) The top-30-per-category emission mostly flags impulse bestsellers.

The twin destroys price adjacency within the category x brand cell, yet keeps rho 0.847 with the card. The main column has R2 0.868 to f_x_i_cmp_sessions_log_14d. The family therefore measures cell-level brand-in-category demand, which is the card's own rival and is already covered by dfs_b, i_brand_share_in_cat_7d and r2p1. It is not price-sibling inheritance, and no fix to the window would change that.

The 'newcomer' definition was censored at the window start, and the debut column was censored by the missing lookback. The corrected version, acquisitions after a fully observed silence of 5 or more days, is an acquisition-composition by inactivity gap. It is folded into revised G4-6 as its long-gap column so that two near-collinear item lifts do not enter as separate families. The remaining overlap with promo and new-reach columns (r1p4, r1p1) is tested there.

The batch test is red because of any_value(). That could be fixed, but the substance does not survive. The loyalty lift is a per-brand constant with R2 0.773 to f_x_dfs_b_buy_per_view_1d. The recency column has R2 0.609 to ub_weight_hl1d. The pair-level part, 'user acquired this brand elsewhere', is largely what the ub_ columns already encode. With 3.9% coverage and a twin whose coverage collapses to 0.16%, the family cannot be tested cleanly and would add mostly brand-popularity noise.

Coverage is only about 3%, and the twin's coverage differs by about 30% (TWIN-BROKEN), so the comparison cannot isolate the path signal. The score has R2 0.50 to f_x_cf_cv2d_cos_max. The same two-hop co-view diffusion is proposed for all users at about 14% coverage by C09/C23, which makes this short-history subset redundant. Only one two-hop family should go forward, and the broader one is the better candidate.
